Installing Prisma

Two packages, three new npm scripts, and a config block — the footprint Prisma leaves on package.json.

Prisma arrives as two separate npm packages, playing two different roles: prisma is the CLI (a devDependency — only needed while developing, never at runtime) and @prisma/client is the generated client your running application actually imports (a real dependency). Figure 2.3 is every change this made to package.json.

// Figure 2.3: adopting Prisma (package.json, excerpt)
"scripts": {
  "postinstall": "prisma generate",
  "db:migrate": "prisma migrate dev",
  "db:seed": "prisma db seed",
  "db:studio": "prisma studio"
},
"prisma": {
  "seed": "node prisma/seed.js"
},
"dependencies": {
  "@prisma/client": "^6.19.3"
},
"devDependencies": {
  "prisma": "^6.19.3"
}

"postinstall" is an npm lifecycle script name — this project didn't call it anywhere, npm runs it automatically after every npm install, guaranteeing the generated client (next-but-one topic) always matches whoever's copy of schema.prisma is currently checked out. The "prisma" block is Prisma's own config: it's how npx prisma db seed knows what script to actually run (the seeding topic shortly). db:migrate/db:seed/db:studio are just this project's own convenience shortcuts for commands otherwise typed as npx prisma ... — covered as they come up.

Note the versions are pinned to 6.19.3 specifically, not left open-ended — Prisma 7 changed how a project's database connection is configured badly enough to be its own, more advanced topic, so this course deliberately stays on the last 6.x release.
